title: Web Scraping Demonstrations in R
text:
This document demonstrates several approaches for extracting structured web data using R.
The examples cover fundamental static scraping techniques using rvest, ethical rate-limiting and domain rule parsing with polite and robotstxt, XPath/CSS element targeting, handling multi-table extractions, and dynamic browser automation using playwright.





Every web scraping example in this document follows the same data journey:
Target URL ──► HTML/DOM Response ──► Select & Target Nodes ──► Parse Text/Tables ──► Data Frame (Tibble) ──► Save Snapshot & CSV







Stage
What happens




Target URL
Define the specific web endpoint or directory listing containing the target data


HTML/DOM Response
Server returns the raw markup tree parsed by read_html() or rendered via playwright


Select & Target Nodes
html_element() or html_elements() locate nodes via XPaths or CSS selectors


Parse Text / Tables
html_table(), html_text2(), or html_attr() extract structured data into memory


Data Frame / Tibble
clean_names() and dplyr transform raw text into analysis-ready columns


Save Snapshot & CSV
write_html() preserves the raw audit snapshot; write_csv() exports processed data







Each scraping script in this document follows a six-step research workflow:







Step
What it means




1. Identify source + inspect DOM
Review robots.txt, Terms of Service, and target page layout via browser Developer Tools


2. Draft selector strategy
Identify unique XPaths (e.g., //*[@id="mwAaI"]/table) or CSS classes (e.g., .wikitable)


3. Request web page
Download HTML with read_html() or establish an ethical session using polite::bow()


4. Extract + clean
Parse tabular nodes with html_table() and clean column names using janitor::clean_names()


5. Save raw + processed data
Write static HTML snapshots to disk for auditability; export cleaned tibbles as CSVs


6. Record provenance
Document the target URL, extraction selectors, scraping timestamp, and session metadata














Term
Definition




DOM Tree
Document Object Model; the hierarchical tree structure representing HTML elements


CSS Selector
Pattern used to select elements based on tags, classes (.class), or IDs (#id)


XPath
Language for navigating XML/HTML nodes path-wise (e.g., //table[contains(@class, 'wikitable')])


User-Agent
Request header string identifying your scraping session to the web server


robots.txt
Text file on domain root specifying forbidden paths and crawl delays for web bots


Static Scraping
Extracting data embedded directly in raw HTML returned by the initial server request


Dynamic Scraping
Automating a browser engine (e.g., Chromium) to render JavaScript and trigger clicks







Both approaches extract web content, but they operate at different levels of execution:








Feature
rvest + polite (Static)
playwright (Dynamic)




Execution
Direct HTTP fetch; parses raw HTML text
Launches full browser (Chromium/Firefox/WebKit)


JavaScript
Cannot execute client-side JS
Fully executes single-page applications (SPAs)


Interactivity
Single fetch; cannot click or type
Simulates clicks, form inputs, and dropdowns


Speed & Overhead
Fast; minimal CPU/memory usage
Resource-intensive; spawns browser process


robots.txt
Obeyed automatically via polite::bow()
Must be verified explicitly (browser bypasses it)


File Downloads
Pulls direct file URLs (href)
Intercepts dynamic browser download triggers


Primary Use Case
Wikipedia, static news, public listings
CDC FluView, interactive portals, complex authentication




💡 Workshop Tip: Steps 3 and 4 directly mirror your code: read_html() pulls the entire document tree into page once, and your custom scrape_by_xpath() function executes Step 4 across multiple table paths.

# Core static scraping
install.packages("rvest")

# Ethical scraping & robots.txt compliance
install.packages("polite")
install.packages("robotstxt")

# Data manipulation and cleaning
install.packages("tidyverse")  # includes dplyr, tibble, readr, purrr
install.packages("janitor")    # clean_names() and table hygiene

# Browser automation wrapper (R interface for Playwright)
# install.packages("playwrightr")

# Table formatting & reporting
install.packages("flextable")





# rvest — core Tidyverse tool for downloading HTML, navigating DOM nodes, and parsing tables
library(rvest)

# polite — ethical scraping wrapper around rvest; checks robots.txt and manages crawl delays
library(polite)

# robotstxt — programmatic checking of domain crawler permission rules
library(robotstxt)

# Core data manipulation: dplyr (wrangling), tibble (modern data frames),
# tidyr (reshaping), stringr (text cleanup), and the pipe operator (%>%)
library(tidyverse)

# janitor — automates column name cleaning (clean_names) and deduplication
library(janitor)

# flextable — builds formatted, publication-ready tables in HTML/Quarto output
library(flextable)








library(rvest)
library(xml2)
library(janitor)
library(dplyr)

# ==============================================================================
# Step 1: Identify source + inspect DOM
# Source: Wikipedia COVID-19 pandemic page
# Target: Primary "Cases by country and territory" table
# ==============================================================================
url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_by_country_and_territory"


# ==============================================================================
# Step 2: Draft selector strategy
# In DevTools, right-click the <table> tag -> Copy -> Copy XPath (not "Copy full XPath").
# The short XPath starts from the nearest element with an ID, so it still works
# when the rest of the page layout changes. The full XPath (/html/body/div[3]/...)
# describes the page after the browser has run its JavaScript, and often finds
# nothing in the raw HTML that read_html() downloads.
# ==============================================================================
target_xpath <- '//*[@id="mwAaI"]/table'

# If Wikipedia edits the page and the ID above changes, anchor on the section
# heading instead, which changes much less often:
# target_xpath <- '//*[@id="Total_cases,_deaths,_and_death_rates_by_country"]/ancestor::section[1]//table[contains(@class,"wikitable")]'

# ==============================================================================
# Step 3: Fetch web page
# Download entire raw HTML structure of the web page into R memory ONCE
# ==============================================================================
page <- read_html(url)


# ==============================================================================
# Step 4: Extract & clean data
# Target node -> parse HTML table -> format headers -> safely drop index column
# ==============================================================================
covid_tbl <- page %>%
  # Target element node using resilient section-anchor XPath
  html_element(xpath = target_xpath) %>% 
  
  # Convert HTML table into an R data frame, filling missing cells with NA
  html_table(fill = TRUE) %>% 
  
  # Convert to tibble, repairing non-unique column names
  as_tibble(.name_repair = "unique") %>% 
  
  # Standardize column headers to clean snake_case
  clean_names()

# Safely drop empty leading index column if present
if ("x1" %in% colnames(covid_tbl)) {
  covid_tbl <- covid_tbl %>% select(-x1)
}


# ==============================================================================
# Step 5: Save HTML snapshot & processed data
# Save raw static HTML snapshot for auditability alongside processed dataset
# ==============================================================================
# Preserves source HTML offline so data extraction can be audited, re-parsed, or debugged if the live site changes 
# save in working directory
write_html(page, "covid_page_snapshot.html")


# ==============================================================================
# Step 6: Record provenance
# Log metadata, execution timestamp, and dataset dimensions
# ==============================================================================
cat(
  "--- DATA PROVENANCE LOG ---",
  paste("Target URL :", url),
  paste("XPath Used :", target_xpath),
  paste("Scraped On :", Sys.time()),
  paste("Dimensions :", nrow(covid_tbl), "rows x", ncol(covid_tbl), "cols"),
  sep = "\n"
)

# Preview extracted data
head(covid_tbl, 20)

# Source: Wikipedia COVID-19 pandemic page
# Target: Extracting multiple data tables from a single page layout
# ==============================================================================
url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_by_country_and_territory"


# ==============================================================================
# Step 2: Draft selector strategy
# Define distinct XPaths for each target table node on the page
# ==============================================================================
# (Copied with DevTools -> Copy -> Copy XPath, as in Snippet 1)

# Target the 2nd matching table node (Vaccine/Timeline table)
path_timeline <- '//*[@id="mwAjg"]/table'

# Define re-usable extraction pipeline function with safety checks
scrape_by_xpath <- function(html_page, xpath_string) { 
  tbl <- html_page %>%
    html_element(xpath = xpath_string) %>%          # Target specified table node
    html_table(fill = TRUE) %>%                       # Parse HTML table
    as_tibble(.name_repair = "unique") %>%            # Convert to tibble
    clean_names()                                     # Standardize column headers
  
  # Safely drop empty leading index column if present
  if ("x1" %in% colnames(tbl)) {
    tbl <- tbl %>% select(-x1)
  }
  
  return(tbl)
}


# ==============================================================================
# Step 3: Fetch web page
# Download entire raw HTML structure into local R memory ONCE
# Passing single HTTP GET request prevents redundant network calls
# ==============================================================================
page <- read_html(url)


# ==============================================================================
# Step 4: Extract & clean data
# Execute reusable function across stored target XPaths against cached HTML
# ==============================================================================
covid_tbl_1 <- scrape_by_xpath(page, path_cases)
covid_tbl_2 <- scrape_by_xpath(page, path_timeline)


# ==============================================================================
# Step 5: Save HTML snapshot & processed data
# Save a single static HTML snapshot alongside individual cleaned CSV datasets
# ==============================================================================

# ==============================================================================

  paste("Scraped On   :", Sys.time()),
  paste("Table 1 Path :", path_cases),
  paste("Table 1 Dims :", nrow(covid_tbl_1), "rows x", ncol(covid_tbl_1), "cols"),
  paste("Table 2 Path :", path_timeline),
  paste("Table 2 Dims :", nrow(covid_tbl_2), "rows x", ncol(covid_tbl_2), "cols"),
  sep = "\n"
)

import time
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright


async def scrape_fluview():
    # ==============================================================================
    # Step 1: Identify source + inspect DOM
    # Source: CDC FluView Interactive Portal
    # Targets: Dynamic SPA app requiring headless browser automation to trigger JS modal
    # ==============================================================================
    url = "https://gis.cdc.gov/grasp/fluview/main.html"

    # Set up local paths for auditability
    save_dir = Path.cwd() / "web_scraping" / "downloads"
    save_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    snapshot_path = save_dir / "cdc_fluview_rendered_snapshot.html"
    raw_zip_path = save_dir / "cdc_fluview_data.zip"
    processed_csv_path = save_dir / "cdc_fluview_data_cleaned.csv"

    # ==============================================================================
    # Step 2: Draft selector strategy
    # XPaths targeting interactive buttons and inputs inside the dynamic modal
    # ==============================================================================
    xpath_header_download = "/html/body/div[1]/header/div[4]/button[2]"
    xpath_custom_option = (
        "//*[@id='downloadDataBody']/ul[1]/li[2]/div/ul/li/label"
    )
    xpath_by_week_tab = "//*[@id='customDownloadPanel']/li[2]/div[1]/div/li/a"
    xpath_modal_download = (
        "//*[@id='downloadDataModal']/div/div/div[3]/button[1]"
    )

    # ==============================================================================
    # Step 3: Fetch web page (Dynamic rendering via Playwright)
    # Launch Chromium browser, accept downloads, and load JS-rendered single-page app
    # ==============================================================================
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        browser = await p.chromium.launch(headless=False)
        context = await browser.new_context(accept_downloads=True)
        page = await context.new_page()

        print("Step 3: Navigating to CDC FluView application...")
        await page.goto(url, timeout=90000, wait_until="domcontentloaded")
        await page.wait_for_timeout(8000)

        # ==============================================================================
        # Step 4: Extract & clean data
        # Execute automated DOM clicks and listen for browser download stream
        # ==============================================================================
        print("Step 4: Executing modal interactions...")

        # Click Download button in header
        await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_header_download}").click(
            timeout=60000
        )
        await page.wait_for_timeout(3000)

        # Select Custom Download
        await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_custom_option}").click(timeout=60000)
        await page.wait_for_timeout(2000)

        # Click By Week tab
        await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_by_week_tab}").click(timeout=60000)
        await page.wait_for_timeout(2000)

        # Set up download listener BEFORE clicking the trigger button
        async with page.expect_download() as download_info:
            await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_modal_download}").click(
                timeout=60000
            )

        download = await download_info.value

        # ==============================================================================
        # Step 5: Save HTML snapshot & processed data
        # Capture rendered DOM snapshot alongside raw download payload and CSV dataset
        # ==============================================================================
        # Save raw HTML DOM tree snapshot
        html_content = await page.content()
        snapshot_path.write_text(html_content, encoding="utf-8")

        # Save binary download payload
        await download.save_as(raw_zip_path)

        # Clean browser environment
        await browser.close()

        # Extract/load raw CSV into pandas (CDC packages extra header rows in download)
        df_cleaned = pd.read_csv(raw_zip_path, skiprows=1)
        df_cleaned.columns = (
            df_cleaned.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(" ", "_")
        )
        df_cleaned.to_csv(processed_csv_path, index=False)

        # ==============================================================================
        # Step 6: Record provenance
        # Document target source, selectors used, execution timestamp, and metrics
        # ==============================================================================
        log_entry = f"""
--- DATA PROVENANCE LOG ---
Target URL      : {url}
Execution Time  : {datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")}
HTML Snapshot   : {snapshot_path.name}
Raw Data File   : {raw_zip_path.name}
Cleaned Data    : {processed_csv_path.name}
Dataset Dims    : {df_cleaned.shape[0]} rows x {df_cleaned.shape[1]} cols
---------------------------
"""
        print(log_entry)
        print(f"✅ Data processed successfully! Preview:\n{df_cleaned.head(3)}")


# Jupyter execution call
await scrape_fluview()


# Pass compression=None so Pandas treats it as a plain CSV text file
cdc_fluview_data = pd.read_csv(
    "web_scraping/downloads/cdc_fluview_data.zip",
    skiprows=1,
    compression=None
)

# Clean column headers
cdc_fluview_data.columns = (
    cdc_fluview_data.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(" ", "_")
)

# View preview
cdc_fluview_data.head()

    processed_csv_path = save_dir / "cdc_fluview_data_cleaned.csv"

    # ==============================================================================
    # Step 2: Draft selector strategy
    # XPaths targeting interactive buttons and inputs inside the dynamic modal
    # ==============================================================================
    xpath_header_download = "/html/body/div[1]/header/div[4]/button[2]"
    xpath_custom_option = (
        "//*[@id='downloadDataBody']/ul[1]/li[2]/div/ul/li/label"
    )
    xpath_by_week_tab = "//*[@id='customDownloadPanel']/li[2]/div[1]/div/li/a"
    xpath_modal_download = (
        "//*[@id='downloadDataModal']/div/div/div[3]/button[1]"
    )

    # ==============================================================================
    # Step 3: Fetch web page (Dynamic rendering via Playwright)
    # Launch Chromium browser, accept downloads, and load JS-rendered single-page app
    # ==============================================================================
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        browser = await p.chromium.launch(headless=False)
        context = await browser.new_context(accept_downloads=True)
        page = await context.new_page()

        print("Step 3: Navigating to CDC FluView application...")
        await page.goto(url, timeout=90000, wait_until="domcontentloaded")
        await page.wait_for_timeout(8000)

        # ==============================================================================
        # Step 4: Extract & clean data
        # Execute automated DOM clicks and listen for browser download stream
        # ==============================================================================
        print("Step 4: Executing modal interactions...")

        # Click Download button in header
        await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_header_download}").click(
            timeout=60000
        )
        await page.wait_for_timeout(3000)

        # Select Custom Download
        await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_custom_option}").click(timeout=60000)
        await page.wait_for_timeout(2000)

        # Click By Week tab
        await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_by_week_tab}").click(timeout=60000)
        await page.wait_for_timeout(2000)

        # Set up download listener BEFORE clicking the trigger button
        async with page.expect_download() as download_info:
            await page.locator(f"xpath={xpath_modal_download}").click(
                timeout=60000
            )

        download = await download_info.value

        # ==============================================================================
        # Step 5: Save HTML snapshot & processed data
        # Capture rendered DOM snapshot alongside raw download payload and CSV dataset
        # ==============================================================================
        # Save raw HTML DOM tree snapshot
        html_content = await page.content()
        snapshot_path.write_text(html_content, encoding="utf-8")

        # Save binary download payload
        await download.save_as(raw_zip_path)

        # Clean browser environment
        await browser.close()

        # Extract/load raw CSV into pandas (CDC packages extra header rows in download)
        df_cleaned = pd.read_csv(raw_zip_path, skiprows=1)
        df_cleaned.columns = (
            df_cleaned.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(" ", "_")
        )
        df_cleaned.to_csv(processed_csv_path, index=False)

        # ==============================================================================
        # Step 6: Record provenance
        # Document target source, selectors used, execution timestamp, and metrics
        # ==============================================================================
        log_entry = f"""
--- DATA PROVENANCE LOG ---
Target URL      : {url}
Execution Time  : {datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")}
HTML Snapshot   : {snapshot_path.name}
Raw Data File   : {raw_zip_path.name}
Cleaned Data    : {processed_csv_path.name}
Dataset Dims    : {df_cleaned.shape[0]} rows x {df_cleaned.shape[1]} cols
---------------------------
"""
        print(log_entry)
        print(f"✅ Data processed successfully! Preview:\n{df_cleaned.head(3)}")


# Jupyter execution call
await scrape_fluview()

    skiprows=1,
    compression=None
)

# Clean column headers

    cdc_fluview_data.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(" ", "_")
)

title: API Demonstrations in R
text:
This document demonstrates several approaches for accessing data through APIs using R.
The examples use different methods, including R packages that provide API access, direct HTTP requests with httr and httr2, JSON parsing, API endpoint discovery, and APIs that require authentication.





Every API example in this document follows the same data journey:
API Request ──► JSON / XML Response ──► Parse & Flatten in R ──► Data Frame (Tibble) ──► (Optional) Save as CSV







Stage
What happens




API Request
R sends an HTTP GET (or POST) to an endpoint URL with query parameters


JSON / XML Response
The server returns a hierarchical, nested key-value structure optimized for web transit


Parse & Flatten
fromJSON() or resp_body_json() converts the nested structure into rows and columns


Data Frame / Tibble
The result is a standard R table you can immediately use with dplyr or ggplot2


Save as CSV
write_csv() exports a flat, plain-text file you can open in Excel or share with collaborators






Each example also follows a six-step research workflow:







Step
What it means




1. Identify source + documentation
Find the API docs before writing any code; understand endpoints, parameters, and rate limits


2. Draft a query
Define fields, filters, and time range explicitly as named parameters


3. Request data
Send the request; respect rate limits; use timeouts and error handling


4. Validate + clean
Check dimensions, types, and missing values before using the data


5. Save raw + processed data
Save the raw API response immediately; save the cleaned version separately


6. Record provenance
Document the URL, parameters, date pulled, and API version













Term
Definition




Endpoint
The URL for a specific resource (e.g., /studies, /drug/event.json)


Method
GET retrieves data; POST submits a query or creates a record


Parameters
Filters appended to the URL (e.g., ?year=2023&state=CT)


Auth
API key, bearer token, or OAuth credential required by some APIs


Rate limits
Maximum requests allowed per second or per day


Pagination
page, offset, or cursor parameters for retrieving large result sets in chunks


Response
JSON or XML returned by the server, parsed into a table in R






Both packages send HTTP requests and handle responses. They differ in style:









httr
httr2




Style
Single-function call
Pipe-based, build then send


Request
GET(url, query = list(...))
request(url) \|> req_url_query(...) \|> req_perform()


Extract
content(resp, as = "text")
resp_body_string() or resp_body_json()


Error check
stop_for_status(resp)
req_error() or automatic


Rate limiting
Manual Sys.sleep()
req_throttle() built in


Pagination
Manual loop
req_perform_iterative() built in


Status
Older; widely used
Current recommended approach







Run this chunk once to install all packages used in this document. Set eval: false after the first run to avoid reinstalling on every render.

# NHANES data access
install.packages("nhanesA")

# Data manipulation and piping
install.packages("tidyverse")  # includes dplyr, tibble, and the pipe operator

# HTTP requests (older, widely used interface)
install.packages("httr")

# HTTP requests (modern, pipe-friendly interface)
install.packages("httr2")

# JSON parsing
install.packages("jsonlite")

# Census / ACS data access
install.packages("tidycensus")

# Table formatting
install.packages("flextable")

# Number formatting (e.g., comma-separated values)
install.packages("scales")





# NHANES survey data — provides nhanes() to pull NHANES modules by cycle code
library(nhanesA)

# Core data manipulation: dplyr (wrangling), tibble (modern data frames),
# tidyr (reshaping), and the pipe operator (%>%)
library(tidyverse)

# httr — makes HTTP GET/POST requests; used for ClinicalTrials.gov and OpenFDA
library(httr)

# httr2 — modern, pipe-friendly HTTP client; used for PubMed and Socrata APIs
library(httr2)

# jsonlite — parses JSON strings returned by APIs into R data frames/lists
library(jsonlite)

# tidycensus — wraps the U.S. Census Bureau API (ACS, Decennial); handles
# geography, variable lookup, and API key management
library(tidycensus)

# flextable — builds formatted, publication-ready tables in HTML/Word output
library(flextable)

# scales — formats numbers (e.g., comma() for thousands separators,
# percent() for percentage strings)
library(scales)









Package: https://cran.r-project.org/package=nhanesA
Data dictionary search: https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/





Quick access to NHANES data
Access the most recent survey cycles without manual file downloads
Merge datasets across modules using participant ID (SEQN)

NHANES organizes data into separate modules, including demographics, laboratories, examinations, and questionnaires. These modules can be linked using the participant ID (SEQN).




# Pull the NHANES demographics module for the 2021–2023 survey cycle.
# The cycle suffix "L" identifies the 2021–2023 data release.
nhanes_demo <- nhanes("DEMO_L")

# Pull the body measurements (BMX) module for the same cycle.
# This contains height, weight, BMI, and related physical measurements.
nhanes_bmx <- nhanes("BMX_L")

The syntax changes across APIs, but the overall research workflow is remarkably similar.



Datasets can be merged using SEQN to create an analysis-ready table.
A data dictionary is important for understanding variable names and coding. For example, RIAGENDR is coded as 1 for male and 2 for female.

nhanes_data <- nhanes_demo %>%
  # Join the body measurements module to the demographics module on the
  # shared participant ID (SEQN). left_join keeps all demographic rows
  # even if a BMX record is missing for that participant.
  left_join(nhanes_bmx, by = "SEQN") %>%
  # Retain only the four variables needed for this example:
  # SEQN = participant ID, RIDAGEYR = age in years,
  # RIAGENDR = sex (1 = Male, 2 = Female), BMXBMI = body mass index
  select(SEQN, RIDAGEYR, RIAGENDR, BMXBMI)

# Preview the first six rows to verify the join and variable selection
head(nhanes_data)









E-utilities overview: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK25497/
e-search endpoint: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK25499/
Usage guidelines: 10 requests/second with an API key; 3/second without





Reproducible literature searches
Retrieve PMIDs and basic citation metadata
Build screening datasets

NCBI requests should follow usage guidelines and include reasonable request pacing for large retrieval jobs.










Workflow concept
This example




Endpoint
https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi


Method
GET


Parameters
db, term (MeSH + date filter), retmode, retmax


Auth
None required for low-volume use


Rate limit
3 requests/second without key; 10/second with key


Pagination
retstart + retmax for batching


Response
JSON → parsed to list → PMIDs extracted to tibble


Package
httr2 (pipe-based: build → configure → send → extract)







The goal is simple: ask PubMed “give me IDs for up to 20 asthma articles from 2023” and turn the answer into an R table.



library(httr2)

# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Base URL for the NCBI E-utilities esearch endpoint,
# which returns a list of matching PubMed IDs (PMIDs)
base <- "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi"

#Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# Define the search parameters:
# db       = target database (pubmed)
# term     = MeSH-tagged search term filtered to 2023 publications
# retmode  = return format (json)
# retmax   = maximum number of PMIDs to return
query <- list(
  db = "pubmed",
  term = "asthma[MeSH Terms] AND 2023[pdat]",
  retmode = "json",
  retmax = 20
)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
# Build and send the HTTP GET request, appending the query parameters to the URL
resp <- request(base) |>      # Creates a request object pointed at the endpoint URL — nothing is sent yet
  req_url_query(!!!query) |>  # splice the named list into individual URL params
  req_perform()               # Actually sends the GET request over the internet and returns the server's response

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Extract the raw response body as a character string
txt <- resp |>
  resp_body_string()

# Step 5 — Parse and Flatten the JSON into R
# Parse the JSON string into a nested R list
dat <- fromJSON(txt)

# Step 6 — Navigate to the IDs

# The parsed list has a specific structure. You drill into it like folders:
# dat
# └── $esearchresult
#       └── $idlist ← this is the vector of PubMed IDs

pmids <- dat$esearchresult$idlist

# 7 - Display the PMIDs as a tidy one-column tibble
tibble(pmid = pmids)









API v2 reference: https://clinicaltrials.gov/data-api/api
Field definitions: https://clinicaltrials.gov/data-api/about-api/study-data-structure





Find trials by condition, intervention, or location
Compare outcomes reporting patterns
Conduct sponsor or phase landscape scans











Workflow concept
This example




Endpoint
https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies


Method
GET


Parameters
query.term (free text), pageSize


Auth
None


Rate limit
Reasonable use; no published hard limit


Pagination
pageToken returned in response for next page


Response
JSON → flatten → tibble


Package
httr (single-call style: GET() → content() → fromJSON())






The goal is simple: ask ClinicalTrials.gov “give me 10 studies about diabetes” and turn the answer into an R table.




# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Base URL for the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 REST API studies endpoint
url <- "https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies"

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# Query parameters:
# query.term = free-text search term (diabetes)
# pageSize   = number of study records to return per page
params <- list(
  `query.term` = "diabetes",
  pageSize = 10
)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
# Send a GET request with a 30-second timeout to avoid hanging on slow responses
resp <- GET(url, query = params, timeout(30))

# Raise an error if the server returned an HTTP error status (4xx or 5xx)
stop_for_status(resp)

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Extract the response body as a UTF-8 text string
data_txt <- content(resp, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8")

# Step 5 — Parse and Flatten the JSON into R
# Parse the JSON text into a nested R list; flatten = TRUE collapses
# nested lists into dot-separated column names for easier data-frame use
data <- fromJSON(data_txt, flatten = TRUE)

# Step 6 — Navigate to the studies

# The parsed list has a specific structure. You drill into it like folders:
# data
#  └── $studies  ← this is the array of study records

# Isolate the studies array from the parsed response
studies <- data$studies

# Step 7 — Display as a tidy tibble
# Convert the list to a tibble for easier inspection and downstream wrangling
studies_tbl <- as_tibble(studies)

# Print a compact overview of all columns and their types
str(studies_tbl)









API overview: https://open.fda.gov/apis/
Drug event endpoint: https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/
No API key required for low-volume use (40 requests/minute; 1,000/day)





Pharmacovigilance exploration
Counts over time, stratified by drug or product fields
Teaching filtering and pagination

https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json


Method
GET


Parameters
search (field-specific filter), limit


Auth
None for low-volume use


Rate limit
40 requests/minute; 1,000/day without key

skip + limit for paging through results

Package
httr






The goal is simple: ask OpenFDA “give me 5 adverse event reports mentioning metformin” and turn the answer into an R table.




# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Base URL for the FDA adverse drug event (FAERS) endpoint
base <- "https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json"

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# Query parameters:
# search = filter to reports mentioning metformin as the medicinal product
# limit  = return only 5 records for this demonstration
params <- list(
  search = 'patient.drug.medicinalproduct:"metformin"',
  limit = 5
)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
# Send the GET request with a 30-second timeout

# Raise an error if the server returned an HTTP error status (4xx or 5xx)
stop_for_status(resp)

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Decode the response body to a UTF-8 text string
txt <- content(resp, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8")

# Step 5 — Parse and Flatten the JSON into R
# Parse the JSON; flatten = TRUE converts nested fields to dot-notation columns
j <- fromJSON(txt, flatten = TRUE)

# Step 6 — Navigate to the results
# The parsed list has a specific structure. You drill into it like folders:
#  j 
#  └── $results  ← this is the array of adverse event reports
fda_df <- j$results %>%
  as_tibble()

# Step 7 — Display as a tidy tibble

Many government open-data portals use Socrata APIs. These APIs support SQL-like query parameters such as $select, $where, and $limit.
Socrata API documentation: https://dev.socrata.com/docs/endpoints



Quick access to many public datasets
Teach select, where, and limit query patterns
Discover datasets through an API catalog











Workflow concept
This example




Endpoint
Discovery catalog + individual dataset endpoint


Method
GET


Parameters
q, domains (catalog); $limit (SODA)


Auth
None for public datasets


Rate limit
Throttled for unauthenticated requests; app token recommended for bulk use


Pagination
$limit + $offset


Response
JSON → flatten → tibble


Package
httr2






The goal is simple: ask the Socrata catalog “find me a CDC dataset about COVID-19 hospitalization”, then pull 100 records from it and turn the answer into an R table.



The following example searches the Socrata catalog for a dataset related to COVID-19 hospitalization surveillance.
The q parameter and domain filter can be changed to search for other datasets.

# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Socrata discovery catalog endpoint
base <- "https://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1"

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# Query parameters:
# q       = free-text search term
# domains = restrict results to the CDC data portal
query <- list(
  q       = "COVID-19 hospitalization",
  domains = "data.cdc.gov"
)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
catalog <- request(base) |>
  req_url_query(
    q       = query$q,
    domains = query$domains
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>   # send the request
  resp_body_json()   # parse the JSON response body into an R list

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Extract the top result from the catalog response
top_result <- catalog$results[[1]]

# Step 5 — Navigate to the dataset identifier
# The parsed list has a specific structure. You drill into it like folders:
# catalog
#  └── $results
#        └── [[1]]
#              └── $resource
#                    └── $id  ← the 4x4 dataset identifier
top_result$resource$id





The goal is simple: take the endpoint URL found in the previous step, ask it for 100 records, and turn the answer into an R table.


Replace the dataset endpoint with the endpoint identified in the previous step. Many Socrata datasets support SODA queries through parameters such as $select, $where, and $limit.

# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Use the dataset identifier from the catalog search above to construct the endpoint
endpoint <- "https://data.cdc.gov/resource/akn2-qxic.json"

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# $limit = number of records to return (SODA pagination parameter)
query <- list(`$limit` = 100)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
resp <- request(endpoint) |>
  req_url_query(`$limit` = query$`$limit`) |>
  req_perform()

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Step 5 — Parse and Flatten the JSON into R
resp_dat <- fromJSON(
  resp_body_string(resp),  # extract response as a character string first
  flatten = TRUE           # collapse nested JSON objects into dot-notation columns
)

# Step 6 — Navigate to the results
# resp_dat is already a flat data frame after fromJSON with flatten = TRUE

# Step 7 — Display as a tidy tibble
as_tibble(resp_dat)








Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data can provide population context for health research, including:

Denominators for calculating rates
Social determinants proxies such as income, education, housing, and internet access
Fine-grained geographies such as tract, ZIP, county, ZCTA, and PUMA
Annual or 5-year series for trend analysis

Common outputs include:

Tract, county, and state estimates
ACS variables and multi-year estimates




The Census API provides a free API key.
Request a key:
https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html
Store the key safely, for example in ~/.Renviron:
CENSUS_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE



The following opens the .Renviron file so the key can be added.

# Open the user-level .Renviron file in the RStudio editor.
# Add the line: CENSUS_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE
# Save and restart R for the variable to take effect.
file.edit("~/.Renviron")





# Read the key from the CENSUS_API_KEY environment variable set in .Renviron.
# install = TRUE writes the key to .Renviron permanently so it persists
# across R sessions. overwrite = TRUE replaces any previously stored key.
census_api_key(
  Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"),
  install = TRUE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)




This example retrieves a basic population estimate for all states in 2023.

# Retrieve ACS 5-year total population estimates (variable B01001_001)
# for every U.S. state using the 2023 ACS release.
# This is a quick smoke-test to confirm the API key is working correctly.
get_acs(
  geography = "state",      # geographic level: one row per state
  variables = "B01001_001", # total population estimate
  year = 2023               # most recent ACS 5-year release available
)







For example:
B01001_001

B or C = table type
01 = broad subject code
001 = table sequence number
_001 = specific line number within the table

Line _001 is commonly the total for the table.











Prefix
Subject Category
Example Metrics




01–07
Core Demographics
Age, sex, race, ancestry, place of birth


08
Commuting & Transit
Remote work, public transit, travel times


11–13
Households & Family
Marital status, family size, fertility


15–16
Education & Language
Educational attainment, languages spoken


17–23
Economics & Finance
Income, poverty, employment


24
Occupations
Employment fields


25
Housing & Living
Rent, home values, utilities, vehicles



A useful resource for searching Census tables is:
https://censusreporter.org




B19013 — Median Household Income
B17001 — Poverty Status by Sex and Age
B15003 — Educational Attainment
B25077 — Median Value of Owner-Occupied Housing Units
B28002 — Household Internet Access
B25044 — Vehicles Available per Household





B tables (Base Tables): Provide more detailed row-level breakdowns.
C tables (Collapsed Tables): Provide broader, collapsed categories.

If a B table contains more detail than needed, the corresponding C table can sometimes provide a simpler overview.














Workflow concept
This example




Endpoint
Census Bureau ACS API (wrapped by tidycensus)


Method
GET (handled internally by tidycensus)


Parameters
geography, variables, state, year, survey


Auth
Census API key stored in .Renviron


Rate limit
Generous; key required for sustained use


Pagination
Handled automatically by tidycensus


Response
Parsed directly to tibble by tidycensus


Package
tidycensus



This example retrieves population estimates by county in Connecticut and calculates each county’s percentage of the state population.

# Step 1 — Authenticate
# Re-register the Census API key for this session (required if the environment
# variable was set after the initial R session start)
census_api_key(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"))

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for and send the request
# tidycensus handles the request, response parsing, and tibble conversion internally
# geography = geographic level: one row per county
# variables = B01001_001 is the total population estimate
# state     = filter to Connecticut counties only
# year      = ACS release year
# survey    = acs5 uses the 5-year estimates for greater reliability
county_pop <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B01001_001",
  state     = "CT",
  year      = 2023,
  survey    = "acs5"
)

# Step 3 — Clean and calculate
county_pop <- county_pop %>%
  mutate(
    # Strip the boilerplate suffix from county names for cleaner display
    NAME         = gsub(" County, Connecticut", "", NAME),
    # Calculate each county's share of the Connecticut state total
    pct_of_state = (estimate / sum(estimate)) * 100
  )

# Step 4 — Display as a tidy tibble
county_pop






build_county_pop_table <- function() {
  county_pop %>%
    # Sort from most to least populous county
    arrange(desc(estimate)) %>%
    # Rename columns to human-readable labels for the final table
    select(
      County = NAME,
      Population = estimate,
      `% of State` = pct_of_state
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      # Format population with comma thousands separators (e.g., 123,456)
      Population = comma(Population),
      # Round percentage to one decimal place and append a "%" symbol
      `% of State` = paste0(round(`% of State`, 1), "%")
    ) %>%
    # Initialize a flextable from the tibble
    flextable() %>%
    # Explicitly set header labels (redundant here but documents intent)
    set_header_labels(
      County = "County",
      Population = "Population",
      `% of State` = "% of State"
    ) %>%
    theme_vanilla() %>%          # apply a clean, minimal table theme
    bold(part = "header") %>%    # bold the header row text
    bg(part = "header", bg = "white") %>%   # white header background
    color(part = "header", color = "black") %>%  # black header text
    # Apply a light gray background to every even-numbered row (zebra striping)
    bg(i = seq(2, nrow(county_pop), 2), bg = "#F2F2F2") %>%
    # Right-align numeric columns in both the header and body
    align(
      j = c("Population", "% of State"),
      align = "right",
      part = "all"
    ) %>%
    # Make the table fill the full page width and auto-size column widths
    set_table_properties(
      width = 1,
      layout = "autofit"
    ) %>%
    # Add a data source note below the table
    add_footer_lines(
      "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 5-Year Estimates 2023. Table B01001."
    )
}

# Render the formatted county population table
build_county_pop_table()

The function can be called again whenever the formatted table is needed.

# Re-render the same formatted table (e.g., after additional narrative text)
build_county_pop_table()

title: API Demonstrations in R
text:
Every API example in this document follows the same data journey:
API Request ──► JSON / XML Response ──► Parse & Flatten in R ──► Data Frame (Tibble) ──► (Optional) Save as CSV







Stage
What happens




API Request
R sends an HTTP GET (or POST) to an endpoint URL with query parameters


JSON / XML Response
The server returns a hierarchical, nested key-value structure optimized for web transit


Parse & Flatten
fromJSON() or resp_body_json() converts the nested structure into rows and columns


Data Frame / Tibble
The result is a standard R table you can immediately use with dplyr or ggplot2


Save as CSV
write_csv() exports a flat, plain-text file you can open in Excel or share with collaborators






Each example also follows a six-step research workflow:







Step
What it means




1. Identify source + documentation
Find the API docs before writing any code; understand endpoints, parameters, and rate limits


2. Draft a query
Define fields, filters, and time range explicitly as named parameters


3. Request data
Send the request; respect rate limits; use timeouts and error handling


4. Validate + clean
Check dimensions, types, and missing values before using the data


5. Save raw + processed data
Save the raw API response immediately; save the cleaned version separately


6. Record provenance
Document the URL, parameters, date pulled, and API version













Term
Definition




Endpoint
The URL for a specific resource (e.g., /studies, /drug/event.json)


Method
GET retrieves data; POST submits a query or creates a record


Parameters
Filters appended to the URL (e.g., ?year=2023&state=CT)


Auth
API key, bearer token, or OAuth credential required by some APIs


Rate limits
Maximum requests allowed per second or per day


Pagination
page, offset, or cursor parameters for retrieving large result sets in chunks


Response
JSON or XML returned by the server, parsed into a table in R






Both packages send HTTP requests and handle responses. They differ in style:









httr
httr2




Style
Single-function call
Pipe-based, build then send


Request
GET(url, query = list(...))
request(url) \|> req_url_query(...) \|> req_perform()


Extract
content(resp, as = "text")
resp_body_string() or resp_body_json()


Error check
stop_for_status(resp)
req_error() or automatic


Rate limiting
Manual Sys.sleep()
req_throttle() built in


Pagination
Manual loop
req_perform_iterative() built in


Status
Older; widely used
Current recommended approach







Run this chunk once to install all packages used in this document. Set eval: false after the first run to avoid reinstalling on every render.

# NHANES data access
install.packages("nhanesA")

# Data manipulation and piping
install.packages("tidyverse")  # includes dplyr, tibble, and the pipe operator

# HTTP requests (older, widely used interface)
install.packages("httr")

# HTTP requests (modern, pipe-friendly interface)
install.packages("httr2")

# JSON parsing
install.packages("jsonlite")

# Census / ACS data access
install.packages("tidycensus")

# Table formatting
install.packages("flextable")

# Number formatting (e.g., comma-separated values)
install.packages("scales")





# NHANES survey data — provides nhanes() to pull NHANES modules by cycle code
library(nhanesA)

# Core data manipulation: dplyr (wrangling), tibble (modern data frames),
# tidyr (reshaping), and the pipe operator (%>%)
library(tidyverse)

# httr — makes HTTP GET/POST requests; used for ClinicalTrials.gov and OpenFDA
library(httr)

# httr2 — modern, pipe-friendly HTTP client; used for PubMed and Socrata APIs
library(httr2)

# jsonlite — parses JSON strings returned by APIs into R data frames/lists
library(jsonlite)

# tidycensus — wraps the U.S. Census Bureau API (ACS, Decennial); handles
# geography, variable lookup, and API key management
library(tidycensus)

# flextable — builds formatted, publication-ready tables in HTML/Word output
library(flextable)

# scales — formats numbers (e.g., comma() for thousands separators,
# percent() for percentage strings)
library(scales)

Package: https://cran.r-project.org/package=nhanesA
Data dictionary search: https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/





Quick access to NHANES data
Access the most recent survey cycles without manual file downloads
Merge datasets across modules using participant ID (SEQN)

NHANES organizes data into separate modules, including demographics, laboratories, examinations, and questionnaires. These modules can be linked using the participant ID (SEQN).




# Pull the NHANES demographics module for the 2021–2023 survey cycle.
# The cycle suffix "L" identifies the 2021–2023 data release.
nhanes_demo <- nhanes("DEMO_L")

# Pull the body measurements (BMX) module for the same cycle.
# This contains height, weight, BMI, and related physical measurements.
nhanes_bmx <- nhanes("BMX_L")

The syntax changes across APIs, but the overall research workflow is remarkably similar.



Datasets can be merged using SEQN to create an analysis-ready table.
A data dictionary is important for understanding variable names and coding. For example, RIAGENDR is coded as 1 for male and 2 for female.

nhanes_data <- nhanes_demo %>%
  # Join the body measurements module to the demographics module on the
  # shared participant ID (SEQN). left_join keeps all demographic rows
  # even if a BMX record is missing for that participant.
  left_join(nhanes_bmx, by = "SEQN") %>%
  # Retain only the four variables needed for this example:
  # SEQN = participant ID, RIDAGEYR = age in years,
  # RIAGENDR = sex (1 = Male, 2 = Female), BMXBMI = body mass index
  select(SEQN, RIDAGEYR, RIAGENDR, BMXBMI)

# Preview the first six rows to verify the join and variable selection
head(nhanes_data)

title: API Demonstrations in R
text:
The goal is simple: ask PubMed “give me IDs for up to 20 asthma articles from 2023” and turn the answer into an R table.



library(httr2)

# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Base URL for the NCBI E-utilities esearch endpoint,
# which returns a list of matching PubMed IDs (PMIDs)
base <- "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi"

#Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# Define the search parameters:
# db       = target database (pubmed)
# term     = MeSH-tagged search term filtered to 2023 publications
# retmode  = return format (json)
# retmax   = maximum number of PMIDs to return
query <- list(
  db = "pubmed",
  term = "asthma[MeSH Terms] AND 2023[pdat]",
  retmode = "json",
  retmax = 20
)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
# Build and send the HTTP GET request, appending the query parameters to the URL
resp <- request(base) |>      # Creates a request object pointed at the endpoint URL — nothing is sent yet
  req_url_query(!!!query) |>  # splice the named list into individual URL params
  req_perform()               # Actually sends the GET request over the internet and returns the server's response

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Extract the raw response body as a character string
txt <- resp |>
  resp_body_string()

# Step 5 — Parse and Flatten the JSON into R
# Parse the JSON string into a nested R list
dat <- fromJSON(txt)

# Step 6 — Navigate to the IDs

# The parsed list has a specific structure. You drill into it like folders:
# dat
# └── $esearchresult
#       └── $idlist ← this is the vector of PubMed IDs

pmids <- dat$esearchresult$idlist

# 7 - Display the PMIDs as a tidy one-column tibble
tibble(pmid = pmids)

text:
API v2 reference: https://clinicaltrials.gov/data-api/api
Field definitions: https://clinicaltrials.gov/data-api/about-api/study-data-structure





Find trials by condition, intervention, or location
Compare outcomes reporting patterns
Conduct sponsor or phase landscape scans











Workflow concept
This example




Endpoint
https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies


Method
GET


Parameters
query.term (free text), pageSize


Auth
None


Rate limit
Reasonable use; no published hard limit


Pagination
pageToken returned in response for next page


Response
JSON → flatten → tibble


Package
httr (single-call style: GET() → content() → fromJSON())






The goal is simple: ask ClinicalTrials.gov “give me 10 studies about diabetes” and turn the answer into an R table.




# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Base URL for the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 REST API studies endpoint
url <- "https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies"

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# Query parameters:
# query.term = free-text search term (diabetes)
# pageSize   = number of study records to return per page
params <- list(
  `query.term` = "diabetes",
  pageSize = 10
)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
# Send a GET request with a 30-second timeout to avoid hanging on slow responses
resp <- GET(url, query = params, timeout(30))

# Raise an error if the server returned an HTTP error status (4xx or 5xx)
stop_for_status(resp)

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Extract the response body as a UTF-8 text string
data_txt <- content(resp, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8")

# Step 5 — Parse and Flatten the JSON into R
# Parse the JSON text into a nested R list; flatten = TRUE collapses
# nested lists into dot-separated column names for easier data-frame use
data <- fromJSON(data_txt, flatten = TRUE)

# Step 6 — Navigate to the studies

# The parsed list has a specific structure. You drill into it like folders:
# data
#  └── $studies  ← this is the array of study records

# Isolate the studies array from the parsed response
studies <- data$studies

# Step 7 — Display as a tidy tibble
# Convert the list to a tibble for easier inspection and downstream wrangling
studies_tbl <- as_tibble(studies)

# Print a compact overview of all columns and their types
str(studies_tbl)

text:
Many government open-data portals use Socrata APIs. These APIs support SQL-like query parameters such as $select, $where, and $limit.
Socrata API documentation: https://dev.socrata.com/docs/endpoints



Quick access to many public datasets
Teach select, where, and limit query patterns
Discover datasets through an API catalog











Workflow concept
This example




Endpoint
Discovery catalog + individual dataset endpoint


Method
GET


Parameters
q, domains (catalog); $limit (SODA)


Auth
None for public datasets


Rate limit
Throttled for unauthenticated requests; app token recommended for bulk use


Pagination
$limit + $offset


Response
JSON → flatten → tibble


Package
httr2






The goal is simple: ask the Socrata catalog “find me a CDC dataset about COVID-19 hospitalization”, then pull 100 records from it and turn the answer into an R table.



The following example searches the Socrata catalog for a dataset related to COVID-19 hospitalization surveillance.
The q parameter and domain filter can be changed to search for other datasets.

# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Socrata discovery catalog endpoint
base <- "https://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1"

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# Query parameters:
# q       = free-text search term
# domains = restrict results to the CDC data portal
query <- list(
  q       = "COVID-19 hospitalization",
  domains = "data.cdc.gov"
)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
catalog <- request(base) |>
  req_url_query(
    q       = query$q,
    domains = query$domains
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>   # send the request
  resp_body_json()   # parse the JSON response body into an R list

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Extract the top result from the catalog response
top_result <- catalog$results[[1]]

# Step 5 — Navigate to the dataset identifier
# The parsed list has a specific structure. You drill into it like folders:
# catalog
#  └── $results
#        └── [[1]]
#              └── $resource
#                    └── $id  ← the 4x4 dataset identifier
top_result$resource$id

title: API Demonstrations in R
text:
The goal is simple: take the endpoint URL found in the previous step, ask it for 100 records, and turn the answer into an R table.


Replace the dataset endpoint with the endpoint identified in the previous step. Many Socrata datasets support SODA queries through parameters such as $select, $where, and $limit.

# Step 1 — Define where to send the request
# Use the dataset identifier from the catalog search above to construct the endpoint
endpoint <- "https://data.cdc.gov/resource/akn2-qxic.json"

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for
# $limit = number of records to return (SODA pagination parameter)
query <- list(`$limit` = 100)

# Step 3 — Build and send the request
resp <- request(endpoint) |>
  req_url_query(`$limit` = query$`$limit`) |>
  req_perform()

# Step 4 — Extract the response body - JSON
# Step 5 — Parse and Flatten the JSON into R
resp_dat <- fromJSON(
  resp_body_string(resp),  # extract response as a character string first
  flatten = TRUE           # collapse nested JSON objects into dot-notation columns
)

# Step 6 — Navigate to the results
# resp_dat is already a flat data frame after fromJSON with flatten = TRUE

# Step 7 — Display as a tidy tibble
as_tibble(resp_dat)

title: API Demonstrations in R
text:
Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data can provide population context for health research, including:

Denominators for calculating rates
Social determinants proxies such as income, education, housing, and internet access
Fine-grained geographies such as tract, ZIP, county, ZCTA, and PUMA
Annual or 5-year series for trend analysis

Common outputs include:

Tract, county, and state estimates
ACS variables and multi-year estimates




The Census API provides a free API key.
Request a key:
https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html
Store the key safely, for example in ~/.Renviron:
CENSUS_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE



The following opens the .Renviron file so the key can be added.

# Open the user-level .Renviron file in the RStudio editor.
# Add the line: CENSUS_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE
# Save and restart R for the variable to take effect.
file.edit("~/.Renviron")





# Read the key from the CENSUS_API_KEY environment variable set in .Renviron.
# install = TRUE writes the key to .Renviron permanently so it persists
# across R sessions. overwrite = TRUE replaces any previously stored key.
census_api_key(
  Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"),
  install = TRUE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)




This example retrieves a basic population estimate for all states in 2023.

# Retrieve ACS 5-year total population estimates (variable B01001_001)
# for every U.S. state using the 2023 ACS release.
# This is a quick smoke-test to confirm the API key is working correctly.
get_acs(
  geography = "state",      # geographic level: one row per state
  variables = "B01001_001", # total population estimate
  year = 2023               # most recent ACS 5-year release available
)







For example:
B01001_001

B or C = table type
01 = broad subject code
001 = table sequence number
_001 = specific line number within the table

Line _001 is commonly the total for the table.











Prefix
Subject Category
Example Metrics




01–07
Core Demographics
Age, sex, race, ancestry, place of birth


08
Commuting & Transit
Remote work, public transit, travel times


11–13
Households & Family
Marital status, family size, fertility


15–16
Education & Language
Educational attainment, languages spoken


17–23
Economics & Finance
Income, poverty, employment


24
Occupations
Employment fields


25
Housing & Living
Rent, home values, utilities, vehicles



A useful resource for searching Census tables is:
https://censusreporter.org




B19013 — Median Household Income
B17001 — Poverty Status by Sex and Age
B15003 — Educational Attainment
B25077 — Median Value of Owner-Occupied Housing Units
B28002 — Household Internet Access
B25044 — Vehicles Available per Household





B tables (Base Tables): Provide more detailed row-level breakdowns.
C tables (Collapsed Tables): Provide broader, collapsed categories.

If a B table contains more detail than needed, the corresponding C table can sometimes provide a simpler overview.














Workflow concept
This example




Endpoint
Census Bureau ACS API (wrapped by tidycensus)


Method
GET (handled internally by tidycensus)


Parameters
geography, variables, state, year, survey


Auth
Census API key stored in .Renviron


Rate limit
Generous; key required for sustained use


Pagination
Handled automatically by tidycensus


Response
Parsed directly to tibble by tidycensus


Package
tidycensus



This example retrieves population estimates by county in Connecticut and calculates each county’s percentage of the state population.

# Step 1 — Authenticate
# Re-register the Census API key for this session (required if the environment
# variable was set after the initial R session start)
census_api_key(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"))

# Step 2 — Define what you are asking for and send the request
# tidycensus handles the request, response parsing, and tibble conversion internally
# geography = geographic level: one row per county
# variables = B01001_001 is the total population estimate
# state     = filter to Connecticut counties only
# year      = ACS release year
# survey    = acs5 uses the 5-year estimates for greater reliability
county_pop <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B01001_001",
  state     = "CT",
  year      = 2023,
  survey    = "acs5"
)

# Step 3 — Clean and calculate
county_pop <- county_pop %>%
  mutate(
    # Strip the boilerplate suffix from county names for cleaner display
    NAME         = gsub(" County, Connecticut", "", NAME),
    # Calculate each county's share of the Connecticut state total
    pct_of_state = (estimate / sum(estimate)) * 100
  )

# Step 4 — Display as a tidy tibble
county_pop






build_county_pop_table <- function() {
  county_pop %>%
    # Sort from most to least populous county
    arrange(desc(estimate)) %>%
    # Rename columns to human-readable labels for the final table
    select(
      County = NAME,
      Population = estimate,
      `% of State` = pct_of_state
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      # Format population with comma thousands separators (e.g., 123,456)
      Population = comma(Population),
      # Round percentage to one decimal place and append a "%" symbol
      `% of State` = paste0(round(`% of State`, 1), "%")
    ) %>%
    # Initialize a flextable from the tibble
    flextable() %>%
    # Explicitly set header labels (redundant here but documents intent)
    set_header_labels(
      County = "County",
      Population = "Population",
      `% of State` = "% of State"
    ) %>%
    theme_vanilla() %>%          # apply a clean, minimal table theme
    bold(part = "header") %>%    # bold the header row text
    bg(part = "header", bg = "white") %>%   # white header background
    color(part = "header", color = "black") %>%  # black header text
    # Apply a light gray background to every even-numbered row (zebra striping)
    bg(i = seq(2, nrow(county_pop), 2), bg = "#F2F2F2") %>%
    # Right-align numeric columns in both the header and body
    align(
      j = c("Population", "% of State"),
      align = "right",
      part = "all"
    ) %>%
    # Make the table fill the full page width and auto-size column widths
    set_table_properties(
      width = 1,
      layout = "autofit"
    ) %>%
    # Add a data source note below the table
    add_footer_lines(
      "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 5-Year Estimates 2023. Table B01001."
    )
}

# Render the formatted county population table
build_county_pop_table()

The function can be called again whenever the formatted table is needed.

# Re-render the same formatted table (e.g., after additional narrative text)
build_county_pop_table()

title: Lesson 2: Web Scraping
text:
What is web scraping?
Web scraping is extracting data from web pages with code. You need it when:

No official API exists for the data
The API is restricted, rate-limited, or paywalled
The data only appears on a public web page (directory listings, public tables, news archives)







ImportantAlways check for an API first



APIs are more stable, better documented, and more reproducible than scraping. Scrape only when there is no API or bulk download. See Lesson 1.


Every example in this lesson follows the same data journey:
Target URL ──► HTML/DOM Response ──► Select & Target Nodes
           ──► Parse Text/Tables ──► Data Frame (Tibble) ──► Save Snapshot & CSV

title: Lesson 2: Web Scraping
text:
Static vs dynamic scraping









Static (rvest, polite)
Dynamic (Playwright, chromote, Selenium)




How it works
Downloads the raw HTML from the server
Drives a real browser that runs the page’s JavaScript


Speed
Fast and lightweight
Slower; uses more memory


Can click and type?
No
Yes: buttons, dropdowns, logins, downloads


robots.txt

title: Session 2: Web Scraping
text:
Teaching notes

Fetch once, extract many times. Steps 3 and 4 of the researcher loop match the code: read_html() downloads the page into page once, and scrape_by_xpath() runs Step 4 for each table. This avoids sending the same request again and again.
Show robots.txt live. Open https://en.wikipedia.org/robots.txt and walk through User-agent, Disallow, and Crawl-delay.
Why save a snapshot? write_html() keeps a copy of the page exactly as it was when you scraped it. If the site changes, you can still check or re-parse your data.
Why static fails on FluView. Open FluView, then view the page source (not Inspect): the data isn’t in the HTML. That’s the moment to introduce browser automation.
Copy XPath, not Copy full XPath. Show both options on the Wikipedia table. The short XPath (//*[@id="mwAaI"]/table) starts from the nearest element with an ID and works in R. The full XPath (/html/body/div[3]/...) describes the page after the browser has run its JavaScript, so it finds nothing in the raw HTML that read_html() downloads. The Playwright script can use full XPaths because Playwright works in a real browser, which is a nice contrast to point out.
Writing code with AI. The last section of the demo shows how to describe a scraping task to Yale’s Clarity platform: the language, the method, the URL, the selectors, and the goal.

title: Session 2: Web Scraping
text:
Known problems

The demo’s IDs can change. IDs like mwAaI and mwAjg are generated by Wikipedia’s software and can change when the page is edited. If a snippet returns an empty result, inspect the table again and copy the new XPath. If IDs keep changing, anchor on the section heading instead. These find the same two tables, and Snippet 1 includes the first one as a commented-out alternative:
'//*[@id="Total_cases,_deaths,_and_death_rates_by_country"]/ancestor::section[1]//table[contains(@class,"wikitable")]'
'//*[@id="Vaccinations"]/ancestor::section[1]//table[contains(@class,"wikitable")]'
If a learner copies the full XPath by mistake, the result is empty ({xml_missing}) and html_table() gives an error. This is a good moment to show the difference between the two copy options.
The Playwright script runs only in Jupyter. It uses await scrape_fluview() at the top level, which works in a notebook but is a syntax error in python scraping_using_playwright.py.
The FluView “zip” is really a CSV. The bottom of the script reads it with compression=None for that reason.
Where files are saved. The R demo writes snapshots and CSVs to the working directory, and the Python script saves to web_scraping/downloads/ (relative to where Jupyter was started). The downloads/ folders are in .gitignore.

Teaching notes

The same workflow every time. After the first two demos, ask learners to name the steps before you run them: endpoint, parameters, send, extract, parse, navigate. The syntax changes between APIs, but the workflow doesn’t.
Drilling into JSON. The demos draw the list structure as a folder tree (dat → $esearchresult → $idlist). Run str() on the parsed object to show learners how to find the path themselves.
openFDA count. openFDA is built on Elasticsearch, so its search syntax supports Boolean logic in the URL. Point out the count parameter: instead of downloading 50,000 records to count in R, count=patient.drug.medicinalproduct.exact returns summary counts directly.
Census denominators. In public health, outcome data rarely comes with population denominators. The Census API provides them. Mention that ACS estimates always come with margins of error (the moe column), unlike administrative counts.
UMLS. UMLS is the “Rosetta Stone” between coding systems: EHRs use SNOMED and LOINC, pharmacy data uses RxNorm, and billing uses ICD-10.
httr vs httr2. The demo uses both on purpose, because learners will see both in other people’s code. Recommend httr2 for new code.

Core vocabulary




Endpoint: the URL for a resource (e.g., /search)
Method: GET (retrieve), POST (submit query)
Parameters: filters like ?year=2023&state=CT
Auth: key/token, sometimes OAuth
Rate limits: requests per time period
Pagination: page/offset/cursor for large results
Response: JSON objects you parse into tables




Note


What is pagination?
Pagination is how an API delivers large result sets in smaller “pages” to control load and response size.
Why pagination exists:

prevents oversized responses
improves reliability
supports rate limiting

GET — retrieve data (most common for research data pulls)
POST — submit a query or create a record (common for complex searches; also for systems like REDCap when writing data)
PUT/PATCH — update a record (more common in operational systems than public datasets)
DELETE — remove a record (rare in public data APIs)




Note


Research norm: you’ll primarily use GET, and occasionally POST for “search” endpoints or authenticated systems.

Pharmacovigilance & Safety Signals: Scan post-marketing FDA adverse event reports (FAERS) for unexpected side effects.
Drug Labeling & Package Inserts: Search structured drug labels for contraindications, black box warnings, or active ingredients.
Medical Devices & Recalls: Query device clearance data (510k), enforcement reports, and recall actions.







🔑 API Quick Facts



Auth: 🟢 No key required for testing (Optional free key raises limit to 240 req/min)
Format: JSON | Endpoint: https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json
Teaching Highlights:

Native count parameter for instant aggregations without downloading raw records
Perfect for teaching API search parameters, filtering, and pagination (limit & skip)







openFDA is built on Elasticsearch, meaning its search parameter syntax allows complex Boolean logic directly in the URL query string.
Highlight the count parameter: instead of downloading 50,000 JSON records to tabulate in R, count=patient.drug.medicinalproduct.exact lets the API do the aggregation server-side and return summary counts instantly!

CDC Open Data — Socrata & SoQL Queries



Key Research Use Cases

Surveillance & Dashboards: Query municipal and national health indicators (e.g., NCHS mortality data, surveillance trends).
Server-Side Data Subsetting: Filter massive datasets on CDC servers before pulling them into R/Python.







💡 SoQL (Socrata Query Language) Syntax


Socrata APIs support SQL-style parameters in the request URL: * $select=date, state, cases — Select only columns of interest * $where=state='CT' AND cases > 100 — Apply logical filters * $limit=5000 — Control payload size
Example Endpoint: https://data.cdc.gov/resource/{dataset_id}.json?$where=state='CT'

Census API — Population Context & Social Determinants



🏙️ Research Use Cases

Population Denominators: Convert raw disease/outcome counts into standardized rates (e.g., per 100,000 population).
Social Determinants of Health (SDoH): Integrate neighborhood-level covariates (median household income, poverty rate, education, internet access, health insurance coverage).
Fine-Grained Geographies: Query small administrative units—from state and county down to ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs), Census Tracts, and Block Groups.
Trend & Disparities Analysis: Compare multi-year American Community Survey (ACS 1-year and 5-year) estimates over time.







📊 Key Datasets & Products



ACS (American Community Survey): Annual sample survey; 5-year estimates offer high precision at small geographies (Tract/ZCTA). Includes estimates (E) and Margins of Error (M).
Decennial Census: Complete 10-year enumeration (2000, 2010, 2020) for exact total counts and basic demographics.









Emphasize that in public health/biomedical informatics, outcome data rarely comes with demographic denominators—the Census API provides those denominators.
Mention ACS Margins of Error (MOEs): unlike simple administrative databases, ACS data always includes sampling uncertainty.

UMLS API — Medical Terminologies & Crosswalking



🩺 Research Use Cases

Terminology Crosswalking: Map concepts across different coding systems (e.g., bridge an ICD-10 billing code to a SNOMED CT clinical term or RxNorm drug concept).
Concept Normalization: Standardize free-text clinical notes or diagnostic terms to unique UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs).
Semantic Relationships: Query parent/child hierarchies, synonyms, and definitions across 200+ biomedical vocabularies (LOINC, MeSH, CPT, etc.).
Phenotype & Cohort Building: Expand clinical query definitions by fetching all related source-asserted codes for a disease or treatment.







📊 Key Metathesaurus Features



CUIs (Concept Unique Identifiers): Universal cluster IDs that link identical meanings across distinct source vocabularies.
Semantic Network: Categorizes concepts into broad semantic types (e.g., Disease or Syndrome, Pharmacologic Substance).






UMLS is maintained by the NIH National Library of Medicine (NLM).
Emphasize that in biomedical informatics, different databases use different coding standards (e.g., EHRs use SNOMED/LOINC, pharmacy data uses RxNorm, billing uses ICD-10). UMLS is the “rosetta stone” connecting them.

Ground Rules for Web Scraping & Compliance




Prefer official APIs and bulk downloads over scraping when available
Respect terms of service, robots.txt, and website usage policies
Avoid collecting PII/PHI or proprietary gated data
Use request delays (Sys.sleep()) and caching to avoid server overload
Document provenance: URL, CSS selectors/XPaths, scraping timestamp, and raw HTML snapshot




💡 What is robots.txt & How to Check It?


robots.txt is a text file hosted at a site’s root URL (e.g., domain.com/robots.txt) outlining rules for web crawlers:

What to look for:

User-agent: Which bots/browsers the rule applies to (* = all)
Disallow: URL paths off-limits to scrapers (e.g., /admin/, /private/)
Crawl-delay: Recommended wait time between requests (in seconds)

How to check programmatically:

R: robotstxt::paths_allowed("https://example.com/page")
Python: urllib.robotparser.RobotFileParser()
🤖 Automated Handling: Higher-level R packages (like polite) and Python tools (scrapy) inspect, parse, and enforce robots.txt rules and crawl delays automatically behind the scenes before making requests!

Data is embedded in public web pages (e.g., directory tables, news archives, regulatory notices)
Capturing visual context or exact web layout is necessary for research auditability

title: Beyond Downloading: Automating Data Retrieval with Web Scraping
text:
Common Research Workflow



HTTP GET Request ──► Raw HTML Document ──► Parse DOM (rvest) ──► Extract Nodes via CSS/XPath ──► Clean & Flatten ──► Data Frame (Table)



💡 What is the DOM?


DOM (Document Object Model): The tree-like structure a browser builds when loading an HTML web page. It organizes elements—like tables (<table>), headings (<h1>), and links (<a>)—into nested nodes that R (rvest) can search and extract.

title: Beyond Downloading: Automating Data Retrieval with Web Scraping
text:
Types of DOM Nodes



Understanding node types helps when targeting specific content during web scraping:








Node Type
Description
Scraping Relevance




Document Node
Represents the entire document root (html)
The starting point loaded by rvest::read_html()


Element Node
Represents an HTML tag (e.g., <div>, <table>, <a>)
Target nodes matched using CSS selectors or XPath


Attribute Node
Represents metadata inside a tag (e.g., href="...", class="...")
Extracted via html_attr() (e.g., getting URLs)


Text Node
Represents the actual string text inside an element
Extracted via html_text() or html_text2()


Comment Node
Represents internal code comments (<!-- ... -->)
Ignored during parsing unless specifically needed









💡 Scraping Rule of Thumb


When web scraping in R: - You locate Element Nodes (html_elements()) - You pull values from Text Nodes (html_text2()) or Attribute Nodes (html_attr())

title: Beyond Downloading: Automating Data Retrieval with Web Scraping
section: Common Data Formats: HTML, Selectors, and Tables
text:
Common Data Formats: HTML, Selectors, and Tables



The Data Journey

What the web server sends back: HTML Document

Semi-structured text marked up with tags (<div>, <table>, <a>), classes, and IDs designed for visual browser rendering.

How R targets specific content: CSS Selectors / XPath

Search paths passed into rvest::html_elements() to pinpoint precise nodes (e.g., extracting links via href attributes).

What R parses it into: Data Frame / Tibble

Functions like html_table() or html_text2() extract text nodes and automatically structure them into rows and columns in memory.

What you can export to: CSV or Database

A clean, flat table ready for dplyr transformations, local saving, or sharing with collaborators.








Note


💡 Bottom Line: Web systems present Visual HTML. Researchers analyze Clean Tables. R (rvest) acts as the scraper that translates DOM nodes into structured data frames.
